Check that _governance_verdict's 'unknown' for import failures matches daedalus.core.GOVERNANCE_STATES

handoff.purpose: Contains promotion logic, governance check, and write wave execution for gated writes.

symbols.name: _promote_one
symbols.note: Wrapper for _promote_one_inner with catch-all exception handler; returns refusal dict on failure.

symbols.name: promote_candidates
symbols.note: Phase 2: promotes list of gated candidates; acquires lock, calls _promote_locked; never raises.

symbols.name: _promote_locked
symbols.note: Creates integration worktree, iterates candidates calling _promote_one, cleans up worktree, returns report.

symbols.name: AUTO_PROMOTE_LEVELS
symbols.note: Tuple of allowed auto_promote levels, currently only 'never'.

symbols.name: run_write_wave
symbols.note: Executes write-mode tasks through gated path, delegates non-write tasks to scheduler.dispatch.

claims.text: Whatever partial state add/commit/gate left behind, the integration worktree must come back to EXACTLY current_head with a clean tree before the NEXT candidate's staleness check above runs -- otherwise that check is comparing against a lie.
claims.why: The claim is about behaviour of code in a try-except block that is not shown (likely inside _promote_one_inner). This chunk only shows the reset/clean after the except.

claims.text: ``_promote_one_inner`` already resets the integration worktree to ``current_head`` on any failure it anticipates; this is the net under that for the failures it does not.
claims.why: The claim refers to _promote_one_inner, which is not in this chunk.

claims.text: ``candidates`` is what Phase 1 (``gate_candidates``) returned, in the SAME order they were submitted -- that order is promotion order too, so 'which candidate wins a real conflict' is reproducible across runs rather than depending on thread-scheduling luck.
claims.why: The claim about gate_candidates and order is not verifiable from this chunk alone.

claims.text: Never raises: every failure mode (lock unavailable, apply refused, cumulative gate failed, base moved and the retry also failed) is a refusal in the returned report, not an exception.
claims.why: The function can raise RuntimeError if _PromotionLock fails with PromotionUnavailable? Actually _PromotionLock raises PromotionUnavailable which is caught. But there is no catch for other exceptions: for example, if manager.create_worktree raises, or if resolve_project raises, or if any other unexpected exception occurs, it will propagate. Also, the docstring claims 'never raises' but the code does not have a blanket try-except. However, the function does catch PromotionUnavailable. But other exceptions are unhandled. So the claim is too broad and broken.

claims.text: ``cancel`` is forwarded to every STALENESS-triggered regeneration (``_reattempt``'s own ``TaskAttempt`` -- see ``gate_candidates``' docstring for what it accepts) AND to the cumulative re-gate's own ``command_gate`` call inside ``_promote_one_inner`` -- the longest-running step in this whole call, since it re-runs the project's whole test command. A cancellation landing there is reported distinctly (``_CumulativeGateCancelled`` in the refusal ``reason``, never conflated with an ordinary ``cumulative gate failed``), and the SAME unconditional ``git reset --hard``/``clean -fd`` that already runs for a genuine cumulative-gate failure also runs for a cancelled one -- honouring ``cancel`` here does not add a new way to leave the integration worktree in a worse state than finishing would; it only shortens how long a stop request takes to land.
claims.why: The claim refers to _reattempt, _promote_one_inner, and _CumulativeGateCancelled, none of which are in this chunk.

claims.text: ``auto_promote`` remains in the call signature so saved build sessions and third-party callers fail closed instead of crashing during migration. The only production-capable value is 'never'; legacy values cannot reach ``promote_candidates``.
claims.why: AUTO_PROMOTE_LEVELS is defined as ('never',). The comment states the only production-capable value is 'never', which matches the tuple. Legacy values cannot reach promote_candidates because run_write_wave coerces them to 'never'.

claims.text: ``(promotion_allowed, governance_state, headline)`` -- read straight off ``daedalus.core.get_governance``, never re-derived here.
claims.why: The claim about get_governance's return format is not verifiable from this chunk; the function does call it and returns the values as described, but the docstring's claim about 'never re-derived' is a statement about intent, not checkable here.

claims.text: That function's own docstring is explicit that a SECOND opinion on ``promotion_allowed`` is how an override sneaks in ('the other gates inform the operator; they do not get a vote on promotion'); this module composes with it by calling it, not by re-implementing the discrimination check. Any failure to even ASK the question -- ``daedalus.core`` unimportable, the call itself raising -- reports the vocabulary's ``unknown``, not a silent True. ``unknown`` and ``absent`` stay distinct facts (see ``daedalus.core.GOVERNANCE_STATES``): this only ever manufactures ``unknown`` for a failure that happened HERE; a real ``absent`` receipt is already reported correctly by ``get_governance`` itself and passes through unchanged.
claims.why: The function catches import errors and call exceptions, returns False and 'unknown' with an explanation. It does not re-implement governance logic. The claim about 'unknown' vs 'absent' is a design statement; the code returns 'unknown' for failures, and passes through whatever get_governance returns otherwise.

claims.text: ``cancel``, when given, is forwarded to ``gate_candidates`` for every concurrent attempt in this wave. ``None`` (the default) is byte-identical to this function's behaviour before ``cancel`` existed: no caller that does not pass it is affected. A caller driving a longer-lived loop (pick -> attempt -> gate -> promote -> re-pick) across multiple waves can pass one shared token/``KillSwitch`` here so a stop request reaches every in-flight ``TaskAttempt`` and every in-flight cumulative gate this wave started, cooperatively, instead of relying solely on the killswitch's process-wide sweep (which still works today with ``cancel=None`` -- see ``daedalus.spine.killswitch``'s own module docstring -- but can race a gate's own poll and report a fabricated verdict; that race is exactly what this parameter exists to close).
claims.why: The claim about forwarding cancel to gate_candidates cannot be verified because this chunk does not show the call to gate_candidates. The function does accept cancel parameter but does not use it within this chunk.

claims.text: ``assignments`` MUST be ``scheduler.accept(tasks, repo_root=repo_root)``'s own return, in the SAME order as ``tasks`` -- the caller (``WaveExecutor.run_wave``) already computed this to decide ``has_writes``/``wave_parallel``. Recomputing it here would still be SAFE (``accept`` is a pure classification -- no persona-cycling or other per-call state feeds it; two calls on the same tasks always agree) but would silently trust two call sites to keep agreeing forever, which is exactly the 'two surfaces, two answers, same instant' drift ``daedalus.core.get_governance``'s own docstring was written to stop. Passed in once, length-checked, used once.
claims.why: The function checks that len(assignments) == len(tasks) and raises RuntimeError otherwise. It uses the assignments to classify write vs other tasks. The claim about ordering and safety is a design rationale; the code does length-check and uses assignments.

claims.text: Returns one result dict per entry in ``tasks``, position-matched -- the same contract ``KairosScheduler.dispatch`` already gives ``WaveExecutor.run_wave`` (see that method's length check immediately after this call). Non-write tasks in the SAME wave (advisory, or bounced to the senior lane) are NOT touched by the gated path: they are delegated back to ``scheduler.dispatch``, scoped to just their own indices, exactly as they would have run before this function existed.
claims.why: The function initializes results list of length n, dispatches non-write tasks via scheduler.dispatch, and inserts results at correct indices. It returns results list. Non-write tasks are not processed by gated path.

claims.text: NEVER writes the primary checkout and never calls ``promote_candidates``. Legacy ``auto_promote`` values are reported as denied input and coerced to ``'never'``.
claims.why: The claim about never writing primary checkout and never calling promote_candidates cannot be verified from this chunk alone. The function does not call promote_candidates in this chunk, but it might be called elsewhere. The claim about coercing auto_promote is kept: the code coerces to 'never' if not in AUTO_PROMOTE_LEVELS.

observations.what: promote_candidates returns report with keys 'promoted', 'refused', 'not_gated', 'integration_branch', 'note'; but _promote_locked returns additional keys like 'inspect' and possibly 'cleanup_error'.
run_write_wave does not handle the case where scheduler.dispatch returns fewer results than expected; it raises RuntimeError.
_governance_verdict catches broad exceptions (BLE001) and returns 'unknown'; this may mask real bugs.

The docstring of promote_candidates claims 'Never raises' but the function can raise if _PromotionLock raises something other than PromotionUnavailable (e.g., OSError) or if other operations like manager.create_worktree raise.
run_write_wave's cancel parameter is documented to be forwarded to gate_candidates but is not used within this chunk; the actual forwarding must happen in a different part of the function not shown.
